# Four types of joints

<!-- STEP id="ball" -->
## Ball and socket joint
The shoulder lets your arm move freely. The rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone, forming a **ball and socket joint**. This joint allows forward, backward, sideways and circular movements. Together with the collarbone, the shoulder forms the **shoulder girdle**, which connects the arm to the skeleton. The hip is also a ball and socket joint.

<!-- STEP id="hinge" -->
## Hinge joint
Unlike the shoulder, the elbow bends and straightens in one direction only, like a door on its hinge. This is a **hinge joint**. The knee is a hinge joint too, and a small bone called the **kneecap** protects it.

<!-- STEP id="pivot" -->
## Pivot joint
Shake your head to say "no" with one hand at the back of your neck, and feel the gentle movement. The skull is connected to the backbone through a **pivot joint**, at the top of the neck. It lets the head turn from side to side, like a doorknob turning in its socket.

<!-- STEP id="fixed" -->
## Fixed joint
The skull is a hard case of flat bones joined together to protect the brain, eyes and ears. Its bones are connected by **fixed joints**, so they cannot move. This keeps the brain safe even when the body moves.

<!-- STEP id="sum" -->
## The four types together

| Joint | Example | Movement it allows |
|---|---|---|
| Ball and socket | shoulder, hip | forward, backward, sideways, circular |
| Hinge | elbow, knee | bending and straightening in one direction |
| Pivot | where the skull meets the backbone | turning from side to side |
| Fixed | bones of the skull | no movement |

**The shape of a joint sets the directions in which its bones can move.**
